August Steffen Möller . Ein Sprachkurs in Krakau hat das Leben des früheren Deutschlehrers verändert. Dort hat er sich in Polen verliebt, und so begann eine unerwartete und verblüffende Karriere. Anfang der 2000er Jahre avancierte Möller als deutscher Kartoffelbauer in einer erfolgreichen Seifenoper zum TV-Star in Polen. Heute gilt er als der humorvollste Brückenbauer zwischen Deutschland und seinem Nachbarn im Osten. Der Kabarettist und Bestsellerautor pendelt zwischen beiden Ländern und arbeitet auch in Zeiten politischer Konflikte zwischen Berlin und Warschau unverdrossen an einer besseren Verständigung zwischen den Nachbarn. Anna Osius Anna Osius kam kurz nach dem Arabischen Frühling zum ersten Mal als ARD-Korrespondentin in Ägyptens Hauptstadt Kairo. Seitdem ist viel passiert, nicht nur in der "Stadt der 1000 Minarette", sondern in der gesamten arabischen Welt. Mittlerweile berichtet Anna Osius aus 15 Ländern über die Lage im Nahen und Mittleren Osten. Für ihre Reportagen wurde sie mehrfach ausgezeichnet, unter anderem mit dem Axel-Springer-Preis, dem CNN Journalist Award und dem Civis Preis. Besonders wichtig ist ihr, auch die Geschichten jenseits von Gewalt und Krieg zu erzählen und den Menschen ein Gesicht zu geben. Welche Menschen ihr dabei besonders nahegekommen sind, kann sie als Bremen Zwei-Live-Gast am 5. September erzählen. Sebastian Krumbiegel Wie Musikunterricht ein ganzes Leben prägen kann, davon weiß Sebastian Krumbiegel , Bremen Zwei-Live-Gast am 12. September , ein Lied zu singen. Die Grundlagen für die Karriere des Musikers wurden im berühmten Leipziger Thomaner-Chor gelegt. Seinem inneren Kompass ist Krumbiegel schon damals zu DDR-Zeiten gefolgt. Mit seinem Widerspruchsgeist eckte er an im strengen Chor-Internat, wo das Leben auf Disziplin getrimmt war. Nach der Wiedervereinigung gaben sich Krumbiegel und seine ehemaligen Mitschüler einen neuen Namen: Aus den "Herzbuben" wurden "Die Prinzen". Der Beginn einer beispiellosen Erfolgsgeschichte mit zahlreichen Ohrwürmern. Aber auch als Solomusiker ist Krumbiegel aktiv, genauso wie als politisch engagierter Künstler in Zeiten des Rechtsrucks. Naheliegend also, dass sein aktuelles Album den Titel "Kompass" trägt. Pasquale Aleardi Letzter Bremen Zwei Live-Gast am 19. September ist ein Schweizer mit griechisch-italienischen Wurzeln. Zum Star im deutschen Fernsehen aber machte ihn die Rolle eines französischen Polizisten: Pasquale Aleardi ist international gut aufgestellt. Den Pariser Kommissar Dupin, den es wider Willen in die Bretagne verschlägt, spielt er so überzeugend, dass sogar Franzosen diese deutsche Serie gerne gucken. So schwer man ihn auf eine Nationalität festlegen kann, so vielseitig gibt er sich auch beruflich, spielt in deutschen Komödien genauso wie im US-Blockbuster oder am Broadway. Und tourt neben der Schauspielerei noch als Musiker. "Die Phonauten" heißt seine Band, ihre unterhaltsamen Eigenkompositionen nennt sie "Antidepressionsmusik". Beste Voraussetzungen also für einen unterhaltsamen Vormittag mit einem Entertainer, den die Presse wechselweise als "heißblütigen Latino" und "charmanten Kerl von nebenan" feiert. When they integrate our services, these sites and apps share information with Google. For example, when you visit a website that uses advertising services like AdSense or Google Ads, including analytics tools like Google Analytics, or embeds video content from YouTube, your web browser automatically sends certain information to Google. This includes the URL of the page you’re visiting and your IP address. We may use the IP address, for example, to identify your general location, to measure the effectiveness of ads, and, depending on your settings, to improve the relevance of the ads you see. We may also set cookies on your browser or read cookies that are already there. Apps that use Google advertising services also share information with Google, such as the name of the app and a unique identifier for advertising. Google uses the information shared by sites and apps to deliver our services, maintain and improve them, develop new services, measure the effectiveness of advertising, protect against fraud and abuse, and personalize content and ads you see on Google and on our partners’ sites and apps. See our Privacy Policy to learn more about how we process data for each of these purposes and our Advertising page for more about Google ads, how your information is used in the context of advertising, and how long Google stores this information. Our Privacy Policy explains the legal grounds Google relies upon to process your information — for example, we may process your information with your consent or to pursue legitimate interests such as providing, maintaining and improving our services to meet the needs of our users. Sometimes, when processing information shared with us by sites and apps, those sites and apps will ask for your consent before allowing Google to process your information. For example, a banner may appear on a site asking for consent for Google to process the information that site collects. When that happens, we will respect the purposes described in the consent you give to the site or app, rather than the legal grounds described in the Google Privacy Policy. If you want to change or withdraw your consent, you should visit the site or app in question to do so. Ad personalization If ad personalization is turned on, Google will use your information to make your ads more useful for you. For example, a website that sells mountain bikes might use Google's ad services. After you visit that site, you could see an ad for mountain bikes on a different site that shows ads served by Google. If ad personalization is off, Google will not collect or use your information to create an ad profile or personalize the ads Google shows to you. You will still see ads, but they may not be as useful. Ads may still be based on the topic of the website or app you're looking at, your current search terms, or on your general location, but not on your interests, search history, or browsing history. Your information can still be used for the other purposes mentioned above, such as to measure the effectiveness of advertising and protect against fraud and abuse. When you interact with a website or app that uses Google services, you may be asked to choose whether you want to see personalized ads from ad providers, including Google. Regardless of your choice, Google will not personalize the ads you see if your ad personalization setting is off or your account is ineligible for personalized ads. You can see and control what information we use to show you ads by visiting your ad settings . How you can control the information collected by Google on these sites and apps Here are some of the ways you can control the information that is shared by your device when you visit or interact with sites and apps that use Google services: Ad Settings helps you control ads you see on Google services (such as Google Search or YouTube), or on non-Google websites and apps that use Google ad services. You can also learn how ads are personalized, opt out of ad personalization, and block specific advertisers. If you are signed in to your Google Account, and depending on your Account settings, My Activity allows you to review and control data that is saved as history by your activity controls when you use Google services, which may include information we collect from the sites and apps you have visited. You can browse by date and by topic, and delete part or all of your saved activity. Many websites and apps use Google Analytics to understand how visitors engage with their sites or apps. If you don’t want Analytics to be used in your browser, you can install the Google Analytics browser add-on . Learn more about Google Analytics and privacy . Incognito mode in Chrome allows you to limit the information Chrome saves to your device when you browse the web. Learn more about Incognito . Cookies are deleted after you've closed all of your incognito windows and tabs, and your bookmarks and settings are stored until you delete them. Learn more about cookies . Using Incognito mode in Chrome or other private browsing modes does not prevent the collection of data when you visit websites that use Google services, and Google still collects data when you visit websites using Google services in private browsing modes. Many browsers, including Chrome, allow you to block third-party cookies. You can also clear any existing cookies from within your browser. Learn more about managing cookies in Chrome . Videos with these audio tracks are marked as “auto-dubbed” in the video description. Viewers can indicate their preferred languages for audio, titles and descriptions, or they can switch between the original and dubbed audio tracks for any specific video. When you upload a new video, dubs will be automatically generated. These dubs will be published according to your publication settings . Over time, we may also generate dubs for previously published videos. Eligibility This feature is enabled by default for eligible creators. If you don’t have automatic dubbing enabled, you can use early access to enable it by clicking Enable in “ Advanced settings .” Your video may be ineligible for automatic dubbing due to the following reasons: Video Length: The video exceeds 120 minutes. Audio Content: The video contains no speech, only music, or very little spoken content. The original audio is in a language we do not currently support. Source Language Detection: We were unable to automatically detect the source language of the original audio. Speech Pacing: The speech in the original audio is too fast, which would result in an unlistenable, sped-up dub. Copyright Claims: The video contains copyrighted content . Automatic dubbing best practices To generate more accurate dubs, confirm you have accurately set your original video or channel language to the correct language when you upload the video. If your video's default language is set incorrectly, its automatic dubs may be mistranslated. You cannot edit automatic dubs. If your automatic dubs were mistranslated, you can update the original video language to the correct language and the dubs will be automatically generated again. Automatic dubbing quality Automatic dubbing helps make information more accessible globally. Over time, dubs may be regenerated to improve the quality, and the quality may not be the same across all languages. Some languages may support expressive speech, which replicates the original speaker's pitch and intonation to produce more natural-sounding dubs. Dubs are generated automatically, so they might contain errors due to mispronunciations, accents, dialects, or background noise in the original video. We may also have challenges translating proper nouns, idioms, and jargon. Other issues may arise with speech recognition, like difficulty matching the voice used for dubbing to the original voice. Available languages Note: We are gradually expanding support for new languages and improving dub quality. As a result, some channels might have access to new languages sooner. For a specific video, you can refer to the Languages page in YouTube Studio for a list of languages available for that video, including which are experimental. Lip sync Lip sync is an automatic dubbing feature that alters the speaker's lip movement to align with the dubbed audio. Note: Early access to this experimental feature is available to select channels, and only supports qualifying videos and languages. Manage lip sync settings Sign in to YouTube Studio on your computer. Click Settings Channel Advanced settings . If the setting does not appear then your channel does not currently have access to the experimental lip sync feature. Click Save . Preview dubs Sign in to YouTube Studio on your computer. Click Content , then select the video you want to manage dubbing for. Click Languages . In the “Language” column, click on the relevant language. In the “Preview” menu under the video, select the relevant language. Play the video. In the “Language” column, click on the relevant language. In the “Audio” row under the description section, select the relevant language. Click on the to show the dubbed audio options menu. Sign in to YouTube Studio on your computer. Click Content , then select the video you want to manage dubbing for. Click Languages . Hover over the relevant language, then click in the “Audio” column. Select Publish , Unpublish , or Delete . Note: When you unpublish a dub, you can choose to republish it or delete it later. title: diamond geezer
text: diamond geezer diamond geezer Sunday, September 06, 2026 Life viewed from London E3 An extraordinary thing is happening tomorrow on Stroudley Walk , a new cafe is opening! We've had fried chicken for a while and a juice bar gave it a go after lockdown, but this is the first time there's been a sitdowner with macchiatos, croissants, hash browns and lasagne. It's called Minnie's Coffee and Food and it made me double-take. It lurks underneath Zellie Emerson House, one of four new housing blocks hereabouts, in a small unit I'd assumed would stay uneconomically empty. Instead our local social housing company have hired out the space as part of their HARCA Café Collective, "an initiative making quality food and drink accessible and affordable to residents and visitors across Bow and Poplar". It's not clear whether Minnie is the owner's name or a reference to Minnie Lansbury the East End suffragette, but given the estate's history and thematic rebrand I'd assume the latter. Apart from the obvious hot drinks the menu also includes breakfast options (until 11am), snacks and a limited range of lunches. I can't remember the last time anywhere round here did a genuine cooked breakfast, and OK there's no bacon but £8 is a pretty good deal. As for lunches each day of the week brings a single meat or vegetarian choice (Mondays curried, Tuesdays stir-fried, Wednesdays filo royale, Thursdays lasagne and Fridays crispy with potato wedges), also soup, also foccacia-based sandwiches, also six quid salads. And yes I know you've probably had this round your way for ages but this is Stroudley Walk for heaven's sake, a culinary dead end since time immemorial. Like most modern food outlets they've not bothered with a website just an Instagram account nobody would ever think to search for. Unnervingly the first post said "Almost ready to serve you!" and that was in June. Also their tagline is "More than just coffee, we’re a community" which I reckon is wilfully unproven given they haven't opened yet. But opening day is Monday at 7.30am and to celebrate they've got a special offer of 50% OFF ALL HOT DRINKS UNTIL MIDDAY. I live nearby and have a kettle so not even Builders Tea for 75p is going to tempt me in, but I wish Minnie well as gentrification finally sparks to life in Stroudley Walk . It's what the incomers who've paid half a million to live in the tower nextdoor have been waiting for, indeed long expected. posted 07:30 : 30 unblogged things I did in September 1986 They didn't have blogs or the internet forty years ago, so here are 30 things I didn't digitally publish at the time. To help you get your bearings I was 21, teetering between university and a job, so chose to delay things by undertaking an extra year's study up north. Mon 1: Sign on at the dole office, but am called to one side to undergo a random check. Thankfully they weren't tough checks in those days. [On TV: London Plus with John Stapleton] Tue 2: My university tutor pops up on Radio 1 Newsbeat talking about vaccinated chickens. Get a phone call inviting me to a job interview on Friday but turn them down because I've decided oil economics isn't for me. Wed 3: Have to go for a job-related medical. Worried it might be a full strip-off but it's no worse than filling a bottle and getting my blood pressure checked. [The supervising medic was called Dr Doodoo] Thu 4: Two friends from university drive over and meet the tortoise, then we go for a walk round Ruislip Lido, watch the water skiing and have cheeseburgers in Wimpy. [Ooh look, I have a photo] Fri 5: My dad takes the morning off work but the man from Anglian Windows never turns up to do the survey and I have rarely heard him so cross. Sat 6: Wimbledon FC beat Watford 1-0 to stay top of Division 1, so I annoy my brother by putting a Womble on the doorstep when he gets home from the match. [On TV: Episode 1 of the season-long Doctor Who story, Trial of a Time Lord] Sun 7: Mum and Dad are debating where to go for a silver wedding getaway next month [it turns out to be a cottage near a radar station in Norfolk] Mon 8: University friend returns and drives us down to the Odeon Marble Arch to watch Aliens. Thoroughly enjoy. [Alas moving up north will squash this budding friendship] [A quick check online and I see he's just retired from his top job in the City] Tue 9: When our nextdoor neighbour moved out she gave us £40 to go out for a family meal, so tonight we go to the Ponderosa Steak House in Watford High Street, a legendary venue. I have sirloin steak and they forget to offer us any free refills. Wed 10: Buy a £299 Sony hi-fi from Tottenham Court Road and nearly collapse lugging it home on the tube. The playing fields of Harrow School, the spire of St Mary's Church and various villas on the slopes below. However Roxeth isn't the cultured enclave at the top of Harrow Hill it's a suburb at the bottom, originally a village to the southwest , hence arguably Harrow-Under-The Hill. It's another example of somewhere that does have a station, indeed it has two, but ever since the bigger one was called South Harrow in 1903 the original name's been ebbing away. It lingers in streetnames, also the local library, park and two schools, whereas the local authority ward of the same name is a modern invention and doesn't quite match the original Roxeth at all. Let's start on the opposite side of the road to my first photo where we find Roxeth's oldest building, a 17th century weatherboarded farmhouse called Roxeth Farm. Alas the owners have sought to shield their property behind a very high hedge so all you can see is a hipped roof from the side and a sash-windowed slot at the front, but it does look to be delightfully wonky. I had wondered if the barn out back was another rural survivor but no, it's one of three pavilions for Harrow School's extensive cricket fields , the Philathletic Ground. According to the whiteboard on West Street the last matches played here were against Merchant Taylors' on 20th June, over ten weeks ago, because one thing that termly fees of £21,990 deliver is a very long summer break. The centre of the village was a four-way junction on the Northolt Road, now a five-way maelstrom called Roxeth Corner. The only building a Victorian would remember is The Half Moon pub, a half-timbered beauty originally named after the shape of the village pond. Its place in history relates to Britain's first fatal car accident in 1899 which, as a plaque elsewhere attests, took place below Harrow School during a descent of Grove Hill. The Half Moon was merely the site of the subsequent public enquiry, hearing how a rear wheel collapsed and two passengers were hurled from their seats, one dying instantly and the other from his injuries three days later. Perhaps unsurprisingly the pub is now an Indian Grill and Shisha Lounge called the Salt Bar, but if you still want a more traditional local try The White Horse a short walk up Middle Hill. The road rising eastwards here is Roxeth Hill, this the route the 258 bus takes to climb from South Harrow to the upper heights of Harrow School. Full marks to the TfL employee who designated the bus stop halfway up with the letters RH . Roxeth Hill is lined by some of the finer buildings erected as the suburb expanded, from small-scale workers' cottages to Arts and Crafts semis, also rustic Christ Church built to cater to a growing population and set back from the main road. Roxeth Primary still educates pupils in an angular hall built for that very purpose in 1851, indeed it's Harrow's oldest surviving state school. I suspect the triple-bend footbridge shoehorned outside is pupil-related, self-evidently over-engineered when a lollipop lady would do, but the upper span does offer excellent views across the rooftops of Roxeth and the plains of Ruislip. By contrast the main road south from Roxeth Corner is architecturally grim . Here former pubs and cottages have been replaced by dubious postwar and postmillennial flats, while the former petrol station has become a drab stacked hotel. The largest presence is Harrow Police Station (alas not Roxeth Police Station), an outdated flag-flying office block whose front desk remains at risk of closure. Arguably the big Waitrose is a big improvement on what was on the site before, namely a mighty tall gasholder with the letters 'NO' painted on the side, this because it was a key navigational landmark on the approach to Northolt airfield. The sole attractive building on this stretch is the clubhouse of the Royal British Legion's Harrow branch which was built in 1927 in Dutch style, its bar and function room even busier visually than the twiddly exterior . Which brings us to the tube station, namely South Harrow, which was opened in 1903 by the District Railway and transferred to the Piccadilly line in 1932. Charles Holden designed the new station building which outside looks to be less of a stunner than usual, but inside has a whoppingly broad ticket hall and a pair of delightful recessed benches halfway up the stairs in case an ascent of 40 steps proves too much. To the north of the station the railway crosses Roxeth Marsh on a low viaduct , hard though it is today to imagine the adjacent avenues as mushy fields. But just down to the left is the source of the River Roxbourne, a minor brook so named because it rises outside Roxeth, and I've previously blogged that in depth so won't dive in again. More relevant is what's been crammed under the arches immediately opposite the station. This is South Harrow Market , one of London's quirkier retail hideaways, essentially two long alleyways serving a warren of tiny bazaars. Most serve up food, so you may need to push past a delivery driver or two, while others will print you a banner, buy your gold or stab needles in your feet. The curse of AI graphics has struck several of the menus, hence I found the Nepalese and Gujarati pictures less convincing than the proper photos at Syria Food. Again it's a shame it's not called Roxeth Market, given it's right on the edge of the original village, but the nominative pull of the adjacent tube station has proved too strong. Continue down the Northolt Road and barely any businesses mention the old place, with only Roxeth Library flying the flag. Even the Chiltern Railways station at the foot of the hill was only called 'South Harrow and Roxeth' for the first three years after opening, after which it was renamed Northolt Park thanks to the creation of a neighbouring housing estate, thus Roxeth's chances of long-term renown were scuppered. For a proper commemoration best see the information boards at the entrance to Roxeth Recreation Ground, these a step up from Harrow's normal design. The text confirms that the name "Hroecs Seath" was first mentioned in monastic documents in 845AD, even if nobody's 100% sure what Hroecs Seath meant, also that several trees in the park are leftovers from ancient field boundaries. You have alas missed this year's Roxeth Show , the revival of a 1970s tradition, because that was in July. Across the railway line from the rec is South Hill Drive, a lengthy avenue whose streetsign has the unusual combination of a 'No Through Road' symbol and underneath "Except by Toll Road". Follow along and all looks normal at first until suddenly the road forks at two white gates , both closed to vehicles unless you have the correct gizmo to open them. The low road enters land owned by the South Hill Estate while the high road enters the Mount Park Estate, another private residential enclave . Both declare that there is NO THOROUGHFARE FOR THE GENERAL PUBLIC but fail to clarify whether pedestrians are included so I strode through a side gate, greeted a resident walking down the hill with a Waitrose bag and chanced my arm. It feels more Surrey than Middlesex, a sylvan climb where villas and minor mansions still feel the need to hide behind high fences and hedges despite supposedly being private anyway. Some have odd names like The Hut (which definitely isn't) or The Site, while others go for supreme Metro-land bland and call themselves Northmount, Southview, Hillcrest or The Oaks. A dozen have been here since the 19th century, a few are totally-out of character modern flats, and I have no idea how residents successfully held suburbia at bay but it's an extraordinary and privileged residential backwater nonetheless. The vehicle with the highest number of Congestion Charge PCNs has a diplomatic plate (290 fines). 25) If you ask TfL to use their office printer to print out every tube map ever produced in colour on A3 paper, along with guidance on how to fold them, they will refuse. posted 08:00 : Belated transport news I missed reporting on several transport stories while I was away so here's a brief catch-up. 🚦 This Saturday the gyratory at St Paul's is being tweaked . The southern end of King Edward Street is being pedestrianised (to create Greyfriars Square) so traffic will have to go a different way and so will local buses. Precisely where the 4, 8, 25, 56, 76 and 133 stop will be altering, and route 100 has already been extended to St Bart's. TfL have produced a ridiculously complicated map to try to explain things (my head exploded), so if you need to catch a bus the City of London's vastly oversimplified version should be clearer. 🚡 It amazes me that every time I do one of these round-ups there's a new thing at the cablecar but there always is. This time it's an interactive audio guide you can listen to on the way across with different stories in either direction. It's narrated by Engi-Bear, the cablecar's lumpen mascot, and produced by an Italian software team called POPGuide . You need to bring your own headphones (and indeed your own phone). The unusual thing is that it costs £1, just £1, when they could have given it away for free or tried to make more money out of it. Upselling has never been so flaccid. 🚇 TfL have added another weekday closure of most of the Piccadilly line to their already excessive roster of downtime, specifically Wednesday 28th - Friday 30th October (immediately before a full line closure at the weekend). Whatever is wrong with the new trains must be proving intractable, given it'll be at least next spring before any member of the public gets on board, fingers crossed. 🚌 London's next dead bus is the 349 which is being withdrawn on Saturday. Expect bloggage. On the same day the latest Superloop route is being introduced, the SL12 from Gants Hill to Rainham. The good news that it'll be free to use for the first week, should you happen to live in the area. TfL have produced a route diagram and a long list of stops in both directions, but not a map because that would be too useful. I cannot overemphasise enough how remote the Rainham terminus is, so expect bloggage there too. 📽️ In mid-August TfL published their Advertising Annual Report , a glossy 49 page compilation of all the showiest campaigns of the last year. It reads like a bunch of talented professionals congratulating themselves on a job well done, but unfortunately that job is to make their advertising more and more difficult to miss. Key phrases include "empowering brands to unlock creativity and turn heads" and "innovation remains central to our shared focus". The scariest project is a "plan to deliver world-first, ten-metre-long digital corridor wraps in selected Elizabeth line stations", i.e. huge moving screens you can't take your eyes off. It's so controversial they've made a full-scale mock-up at UCL "to evaluate how digital corridor wraps might impact the experience of customers who are neurodivergent or disabled". See photo. They hope the research will show any potential impacts can be mitigated, but I hope someone will grow a conscience and halt the introduction of these massive digital intrusions. Advertising targets shouldn't be fixated on increasing distraction, forever designing formats it's more and more impossible to take our eyes off. 📱 The report also suggests you could be seeing a lot more adverts on TfL Go in future. At present the app generates 76 million page views a month but only made £5,000 in revenue last year, thus "TfL Go represents a significant long-term growth opportunity". 🚌 If you enjoy those free heritage bus days when the London Bus Museum floods a historic route with vintage vehicles, the list of planned events has extended. Route 85: 2nd October 2027. posted 07:00 : Monday, August 31, 2026 THE BASQUE COUNTRY Bilbao & its transport [70 photos] San Sebastián & cideria [50 photos] Biarritz France [40 photos] VITORIA- GASTEIZ & total solar eclipse [60 photos] DLR trains salt valley La Rioja [←40 photos→] Pamplona posted 09:00 : This blog loves a boundary and the border between Spain and France is one of the more significant. It's 425 miles long, was finally settled in 1856 and mostly follows the drainage divide of the Pyrenees. At its western end it divides the towns of Irun (Spain) and Hendaye (France), or more precisely the Spanish town of Hondarribia and the French suburb of Zokuburu. If you stand in Hondarribia's main square and look down the hill you can see where the border ends at the mouth of the river Bidasoa . Spain's on the left, France on the right. There are many ways to cross the border here. By road European route E5 crosses the border four miles upstream at the Zubi Nazioartekoa . On the Spanish side the autoroute is designated AP-8 , then morphs into the A63 to Bordeaux in the middle of the bridge. The French side immediately welcomes drivers with a toll booth, or if viewed the other way charges drivers for leaving the country. There are no passport checks or customs, nor at the two non-motorway bridges between the two sides. We returned via the more minor Santiago Bridge, freely crossing thanks to EU accords which have made the former queues obsolete. That said we did pass French gendarmes setting up beside the road ready to spot-check inbound traffic, so maybe be careful what you choose to take in or out. By rail A 120m-long railway bridge links Spanish railways to France, which is awkward because the countries have very different gauges. There are thus a heck of a lot of marshalling yards on either side to aid transfer of rolling stock. A parallel bridge carries the Euskotren metro train from San Sebastián but this travels only 400m into France before terminating at Hendaye station. Long distance rail travellers need to transfer to the Euskotren to make their connection, or else lug their luggage for a mile and a half via the Santiago Bridge. We had hoped to visit Biarritz by train but the connecting faff (and oddly infrequent services on the French side) made it far better to drive instead. [The Man in Seat 61] By boat The lowest crossing of the border is the ferry that's been shuttling between Hondarribia and Hendaye since 1993. The service crosses Txingudi Bay in seven minutes flat for the ferry reasonable fare of €2.50. The jetty was only a ten minute walk from where I took today's first photo so I was sorely tempted to make a pointless border crossing just for the sake of it. My travelling companions instead prioritised lunch so we settled at Mika Jatetxea for pintxos and pork rib with orange and cheddar sauce and I missed my chance. Also best not risk a trip to a foreign country when your plane leaves in three hours, so Hondarribia's lovely walled town was a far safer bet. By air For reasons of flatness San Sebastián's airport is 10 miles east of the city in Hondarribia, built on reclaimed land in the Bidasoa estuary. For reasons of space the runway is short so gets only a handful of flights daily, all in small planes including a few weekly returns to London City Airport. For reasons of geography the runway is incredibly close to the mid-stream national border, the centre of the runway barely 100m away, indeed only a few seconds after take-off you've already entered French airspace. If you remember the very first photo I showed you at the start of my holiday travelogue , taken from the window of my departing plane, that had Spain in the foreground, France in the background and the Santiago Bridge inbetween. One holiday, two countries, and somehow it's taken me longer to write up than I spent there. posted 08:00 : If you've driven all the way to France you might as well stop somewhere else on the way back. ✉ A postcard from Saint-Jean-de-Luz On my summer holidays we went to Saint-Jean-de-Luz which is in France but only just. It is six miles from Spain on the coast and it has a big bay and ice creams. It is not a fun place to park but we managed. The place to go is the beach , it is long and very sandy. A lot of people were playing beach volleyball because there is a lot of space . The sun was starting to set over the fort and lighthouse at the far end of the bay and it was very pretty . But nobody was in the sea because the purple flag was flying. The purple flag means JELLYFISH! or in this case Portuguese men o' war because they had invaded . I have never seen a purple flag before it is serious, if one stings you in precisely the wrong place you could die. The lifeguards sounded a big horn when they saw someone wading in. It must be gutting if you come here for a week's holiday and a blue bag of venom stops you going in the water. The biggest building on the promenade is the casino , there is always a casino although this one closed a while back. It has a boardwalk and a pergola and little shops. We bought ice creams from a Glaces Lopez van on the promenade, they've been going since 1924. I had citron in a cornet, it was yummy and only €1.70 which is a total bargain. We also bought Gâteaux Basques from Maison Adam in the high street but only the small ones, I liked the custard filling best. Maison Adam are most famous for their macarons , they once made them for the wedding of Louis XIV and Marie Theresa of Spain which took place here in Saint-Jean-de-Luz in 1660. Now that's an origin story! The high street is proper characterful, all narrow with brightly-painted shutters. It's also a bit designer in places, such is the tourist clientele, although if you buy surf gear you have to go out of town to use it because the bay doesn't get big waves. At the lower end are a lot of outdoor bar tables, London has nothing on this, also the marina where the nice boats are. The smart dockfront museum is the House of the Infanta , this because Marie Theresa spent the night before her wedding here ( Maison Louis XIV is just round the corner). The harbour is also the mouth of the Nivelle but it is not a famous river. On the way back to the car we passed the public fronton , which is the place where they play pelote . I first learned about pelote in my Tricolore textbook and now here I was watching two Basque lads hurling a ball really hard against a wall using their long curved xistera. Then they had to stop playing because a truck arrived with tree trunks for tonight's Basque Strength event , a display of athletic sawing, bale lifting, sack racing and tug of war. We didn't have time to stay but what with the pelote, games and gâteaux we had learned that Saint-Jean-de-Luz is just as Basque as towns the other side of the Spanish border.
